analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1935 law restricting utility holding companies, replacing strict oversight with records-access rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, a Depression-era law that puts structural limits on companies that own electric and gas utilities through holding company systems. In its place, the bill would set up a much lighter regime: federal and state regulators could look at the books and records of companies in a holding company system when needed to set rates, but the Securities and Exchange Commission's registration and approval system would be eliminated, and federal regulators would be required to exempt many holding companies from even the records-access requirements. The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce subcommittee to which it was referred.
analysis.who_benefits: Utility holding companies and their affiliates gain most: they would be freed from the 1935 Act's registration requirements, approval of mergers and acquisitions, and limits on what non-utility businesses a utility system can own, keeping only an obligation to open their books to regulators when costs matter to rates. Many holding companies would also be exempted from the records-access rules by a mandatory federal rule or a regulator's relevance finding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electric and gas utility holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 effective 12 months after enactment, ending the Securities and Exchange Commission's registration and structural oversight of utility holding companies [S2][S3].

Replaces it with a system in which federal and state commissions get access to holding company books and records relevant to utility rates, but the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission must exempt qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies from the records requirements, and must exempt any person or transaction it finds irrelevant to jurisdictional rates [S2][S3].

Preserves the ability of federal and state regulators to decide whether a utility may recover in rates the costs of transactions with associate companies, and transfers the relevant records from the SEC to FERC [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Utility ratepayers bear the risk side of the trade: the 1935 Act's limits on holding company structure, affiliate dealings, and non-utility investments disappear, leaving only records-access and rate-recovery review to protect them from costs shifted into utility rates through affiliate transactions. The Securities and Exchange Commission loses the records and role it held under the old law.

drawbacks.text: The 1935 Act did more than provide records access: it required SEC registration, restricted holding company structures and acquisitions, and limited non-utility operations. Replacing all of that with books-and-records access alone leaves ratepayers relying on regulators to detect, transaction by transaction, costs that were pushed into utility rates through affiliate companies [S2][S3].

The bill requires FERC to exempt broad categories of holding companies, and to exempt any person or transaction it deems irrelevant to rates, which could remove even the records-access check for much of a holding company system [S2][S3].

It requires FERC to issue a final exemption rule within 90 days of enactment and all implementing regulations within 12 months, a timeline that would give regulators little time to build a replacement oversight structure before the 1935 Act is repealed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair argument that parts of the 1935 Act were outdated for a modern energy industry, and the bill keeps some rate-protection tools. But the core trade is one-sided: a holding company gets full freedom to structure mergers, acquisitions, and affiliate deals without SEC approval, while ratepayer protection shrinks to looking at paperwork after costs are incurred, with broad mandatory exemptions. The bill was designed to deliver what utility holding companies had long sought from repeal, and its consumer provisions are weaker than the safeguards it removes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee in April 2003, and the subcommittee never acted on it before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2003 by Rep. Chip Pickering, joined by Rep. Edolphus Towns, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
A week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it stayed for the remainder of the 108th Congress with no further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
It had only 3 cosponsors (2 Democrats and 1 Republican) [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utility ratepayers kept the 1935 Act's structural safeguards for the rest of the Congress. Utility holding companies had to wait until a later Congress to get the repeal they sought through a broader energy bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ratepayers, for the remainder of the 108th Congress

for.name: Rep. Charles W. "Chip" Pickering
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 1935 Public Utility Holding Company Act and replace it with a lighter records-access regime.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Joined as the Democratic co-lead on the day of introduction; the bill drew 3 cosponsors total (2 D, 1 R) [S4].

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.role: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 10, 2003 and never reported it out or held action on it before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and co-led by a Democrat with a small bipartisan cosponsor list (3 total: 2 D, 1 R), and it never reached a vote, so no partisan voting pattern exists in the record.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utility holding companies
industries.note: Repeal of the 1935 Act frees them from SEC registration, structural limits, and acquisition approvals, keeping only books-and-records access where rates are affected, with broad exemption authority on top. Ratepayer protection from cost-shifting through affiliate transactions would shrink from structural rules to after-the-fact paperwork review.
They gain federal backing for access to holding company records anywhere in the system when needed for rate proceedings, but lose the SEC's structural oversight of the companies they regulate.
The bill transfers PUHCA oversight, and the related records, from the SEC to FERC, ending a long-standing SEC regulatory role over utility holding companies.
